title: When Should I See A GP About Headaches?
h1: When Should I See A GP About Headaches?
description: Headaches are common, but their pattern matters.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when should i see a gp about headaches
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Headache & Migraine When Should I See A GP About Headaches? Headaches are common, but their pattern matters. An occasional mild headache may settle with rest and simple care; headaches that return often, change or affect daily life deserve a closer look. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Headaches are common, but their pattern matters. An occasional mild headache may settle with rest and simple care; headaches that return often, change or affect daily life deserve a closer look. What Is It? Headache describes pain felt in the head or neck. Common patterns include tension-type headaches and migraine, but infections, medicines, sleep, dehydration and other conditions can contribute. Knowing when a headache started, how long it lasted and what came with it is more useful than trying to diagnose yourself. Headaches that disrupt activities A new or changing headache pattern Regular use of headache pain medication Should I Be Concerned? Arrange an appointment if headaches are becoming more frequent, you need pain relief repeatedly, or they interfere with work, study or sleep. Headaches that are different from your usual pattern, or begin in pregnancy, require particular attention. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 for a sudden extremely severe headache, or a headache with weakness, confusion, seizures, collapse, a stiff neck with fever, or new vision loss. A new headache after a serious head injury needs urgent assessment. Do not wait for an ordinary appointment in these situations. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can review the headache history, examine you, check medicines and other health factors, and decide whether further investigations or specialist assessment are necessary. A headache diary recording days, symptoms, medicines and possible triggers can make the appointment more useful. A headache diary, list of medicines and details of new associated symptoms can help make the consultation more useful. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Should I keep a headache diary? Yes. Recording timing, severity, sleep, menstrual patterns, associated symptoms and medication use can help identify a pattern without assuming the cause. Does every headache need a scan? No. A GP considers symptoms and examination findings before deciding whether imaging is appropriate. Many common headache patterns do not require a scan. title: Migraine or Headache? How to Tell the Difference
h1: Migraine Or Headache: How Do I Tell The Difference?
description: People often use the word “headache” for any head pain, but migraine has characteristic features and may need a different management approach.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles migraine or headache how do i tell the difference
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Headache & Migraine Migraine Or Headache: How Do I Tell The Difference? People often use the word “headache” for any head pain, but migraine has characteristic features and may need a different management approach. A diagnosis depends on the whole symptom history, not one symptom alone. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction People often use the word “headache” for any head pain, but migraine has characteristic features and may need a different management approach. A diagnosis depends on the whole symptom history, not one symptom alone. What Is It? Migraine is a neurological condition that can cause moderate or severe headache, nausea and sensitivity to light or sound. Some people experience temporary visual or sensory symptoms called aura. Tension-type headache more often feels like pressure or tightness, although features can overlap. Throbbing or disabling head pain Nausea or sensitivity to light and sound Visual disturbances before or during an episode Should I Be Concerned? A headache that repeatedly forces you to stop activities, involves nausea, or follows a similar disabling pattern may suggest migraine. New aura-like symptoms should not automatically be attributed to migraine, particularly if they differ from anything you have experienced before. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 for new facial drooping, weakness, trouble speaking, sudden severe headache or other symptoms that could indicate stroke. Urgent assessment is also necessary for sudden vision loss, confusion or seizure, even if you have a history of migraine. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can discuss whether the pattern fits migraine, look for alternative causes and talk through acute treatment, prevention, medication overuse and practical triggers. If migraine is frequent or difficult to control, your GP may discuss preventive medicines or referral. A headache diary, list of medicines and details of new associated symptoms can help make the consultation more useful. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can migraine happen without severe headache? Yes. Some people have aura or other migraine-related symptoms with little or no head pain; new neurological symptoms still need medical assessment. Are migraine and tension headache treated the same way? Not always. The choice of medicine and prevention depends on the headache type, frequency, health history and other medicines. title: What Causes Frequent Headaches?
description: Frequent headaches can have several contributing factors. Identifying a pattern is often more helpful than focusing on one suspected trigger.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles what causes frequent headaches
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Headache & Migraine What Causes Frequent Headaches? Frequent headaches can have several contributing factors. Identifying a pattern is often more helpful than focusing on one suspected trigger. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Frequent headaches can have several contributing factors. Identifying a pattern is often more helpful than focusing on one suspected trigger. What Is It? Recurring headaches may relate to migraine, tension-type headache, sleep disruption, neck tension, stress, dehydration or certain medicines. Taking pain medicines too often can itself contribute to medication-overuse headache. Persistent headaches occasionally have another medical cause that needs investigation. Headache days increasing Headaches after frequent pain relief Poor sleep or symptoms affecting concentration Should I Be Concerned? It is worth arranging review when headaches increase over weeks, keep coming back, interfere with daily life or need regular medicine. Tell your GP about caffeine, supplements, over-the-counter medicines, menstrual changes, sleep and any new neurological symptoms. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? A headache with sudden onset and extreme severity, stroke-like symptoms, fever with neck stiffness, seizures, or reduced consciousness is an emergency: call 000. Seek prompt medical review after head injury or with a rapidly changing pattern. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can check for common headache types, examine the nervous system, discuss safe pain-medicine use and work with you on treatment and follow-up. Blood tests or scans are considered only when the clinical picture supports them. A headache diary, list of medicines and details of new associated symptoms can help make the consultation more useful. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can taking pain relief make headaches worse? Using some headache medicines too often can contribute to medication-overuse headaches. Ask a GP or pharmacist before changing regular medicines. Should I stop caffeine suddenly? Not necessarily. Sudden caffeine withdrawal can cause headache; discuss gradual adjustments if caffeine appears relevant. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources offer further general information. Recommendations and eligibility can change; your GP can explain how guidance applies to you. title: When Is a Headache an Emergency?
h1: When Is A Headache An Emergency?
description: Most headaches are not life-threatening. A small number have warning features that should change what you do next.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when is a headache an emergency
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Headache & Migraine When Is A Headache An Emergency? Most headaches are not life-threatening. A small number have warning features that should change what you do next. Recognising these signs is more important than trying to label the headache. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Most headaches are not life-threatening. A small number have warning features that should change what you do next. Recognising these signs is more important than trying to label the headache. What Is It? A sudden “thunderclap” headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds or minutes may reflect a serious problem. Severe headache can also accompany meningitis, stroke, bleeding, a serious head injury or other conditions requiring emergency assessment. Sudden severe headache New weakness, confusion, seizure or speech changes Headache with fever and stiff neck Should I Be Concerned? Be concerned about new weakness, difficulty speaking, confusion, collapse, a seizure, sudden vision changes, severe neck stiffness, or fever with a severe headache. The combination of symptoms and how quickly they appear matters. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 immediately for a sudden extremely severe headache or a headache with stroke-like symptoms, seizure, fainting or reduced consciousness. Do not drive yourself. If you are pregnant and develop a severe or unusual headache, seek urgent obstetric or medical advice. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Emergency clinicians assess dangerous causes first. After urgent conditions have been excluded, a GP can help with follow-up, headache prevention and ongoing treatment. Digital information cannot safely rule out an emergency. A headache diary, list of medicines and details of new associated symptoms can help make the consultation more useful. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Should I wait to see if the pain goes away? Not if the headache is sudden and extremely severe or comes with neurological warning signs. Call 000. Can I book a normal GP appointment instead? For ordinary recurring headache patterns, a GP appointment is appropriate. For emergency warning signs, use emergency services rather than online booking. title: Why Won’t My Cough Go Away?
h1: Why Won’t My Cough Go Away?
description: Coughing can continue for some time after a respiratory infection.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles why won t my cough go away
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Cough & Sore Throat Why Won’t My Cough Go Away? Coughing can continue for some time after a respiratory infection. A cough that is not improving, lasts several weeks or comes with other symptoms deserves medical attention. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Coughing can continue for some time after a respiratory infection. A cough that is not improving, lasts several weeks or comes with other symptoms deserves medical attention. What Is It? Cough is the body’s way of clearing the airways. After a cold or flu, airway irritation may linger. Other causes include asthma, post-nasal drip, reflux, smoking exposure, some blood-pressure medicines or underlying lung disease. The timing and type of cough can help narrow the possibilities. Cough lasting more than four weeks A persistent night-time cough Cough with breathlessness or weight loss Should I Be Concerned? Arrange GP review for a cough lasting more than four weeks, worsening symptoms, recurrent cough, disrupted sleep, unexplained fever or weight loss, or symptoms that seem different from a usual post-viral cough. Mention any smoking history or new medication. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 for severe difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, bluish lips, marked drowsiness or collapse. Coughing up blood, new significant breathlessness or chest pain warrants prompt medical assessment. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP may examine the chest, review medicines and allergies, check oxygen levels when needed and consider tests such as spirometry or chest imaging. Management targets the underlying cause rather than routinely prescribing antibiotics. Before attending, note how long symptoms have lasted, whether fever or breathlessness is present and which medicines you take. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions How long can a post-viral cough last? Some coughs persist after other cold symptoms settle. If a cough lasts several weeks or is worsening, arrange a GP review rather than assuming it is harmless. Do antibiotics help every cough? No. Antibiotics do not treat viral infections. A GP determines whether there is evidence of a bacterial infection or another condition. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources offer further general information. title: What Causes a Persistent Cough?
description: A persistent cough is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Looking at possible causes helps a GP select useful tests and avoid unnecessary treatment.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles what causes a persistent cough
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Cough & Sore Throat What Causes A Persistent Cough? A persistent cough is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Looking at possible causes helps a GP select useful tests and avoid unnecessary treatment. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction A persistent cough is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Looking at possible causes helps a GP select useful tests and avoid unnecessary treatment. What Is It? An adult cough lasting more than eight weeks is generally described as chronic. Common causes include asthma, upper airway cough syndrome, reflux and medication effects. Less common causes include chronic lung disease, infection or a more serious chest condition. Cough for eight weeks or longer Wheeze, nasal drip or reflux alongside cough A cough after a change of medicine Should I Be Concerned? A dry cough after starting an ACE-inhibitor blood-pressure medicine is worth mentioning, but never stop prescribed medicine without advice. Wheezing, reflux symptoms, nasal congestion, smoking history, workplace exposures and whether the cough is wet or dry also matter. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Seek urgent care if coughing is accompanied by severe breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or rapid deterioration. For life-threatening breathing difficulty call 000. Routine chronic-cough investigations should not delay urgent assessment. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can take a structured history, listen to the chest and decide whether spirometry, chest X-ray or treatment trials are appropriate. The plan may include reviewing medication or assessing asthma, reflux and nasal symptoms. Before attending, note how long symptoms have lasted, whether fever or breathlessness is present and which medicines you take. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can reflux cause coughing without heartburn? Yes. Reflux-related irritation can contribute to cough even when classic heartburn is not obvious. Assessment is important before attributing a persistent cough to reflux. Do I need a chest X-ray? Not everyone does. A GP decides based on duration, examination, risk factors and warning symptoms. title: Sore Throat: When Should I See A Doctor?
h1: Sore Throat: When Should I See A Doctor?
description: A sore throat is often short-lived, but severe symptoms and difficulties swallowing or breathing need attention.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles sore throat when should i see a doctor
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Cough & Sore Throat Sore Throat: When Should I See A Doctor? A sore throat is often short-lived, but severe symptoms and difficulties swallowing or breathing need attention. The cause cannot always be judged by appearance alone. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction A sore throat is often short-lived, but severe symptoms and difficulties swallowing or breathing need attention. The cause cannot always be judged by appearance alone. What Is It? Most sore throats occur with viral infections. Bacterial infection, glandular fever, irritation and other illnesses can also cause throat pain. Symptoms may include pain on swallowing, fever, swollen glands, cough, hoarseness and fatigue. Persistent severe throat pain Fever and swollen neck glands Difficulty swallowing fluids Should I Be Concerned? See a GP if symptoms are unusually severe, not improving after several days, recur frequently, or come with a rash, persistent fever or significant dehydration. Children and people with reduced immunity may need a lower threshold for assessment. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 for breathing difficulty, inability to swallow saliva, severe swelling of the throat or rapidly worsening illness. A child who is drooling, struggling to breathe or becoming unusually drowsy needs emergency assessment. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can examine the throat and neck, assess hydration and discuss whether testing or antibiotics are warranted. Advice about appropriate pain relief and fluids can help while the illness resolves. Before attending, note how long symptoms have lasted, whether fever or breathlessness is present and which medicines you take. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can I treat a sore throat at home? Many mild sore throats improve with fluids, rest and suitable pain relief. Seek review if symptoms persist or warning features develop. Should I ask for antibiotics? Antibiotics help selected bacterial infections, not routine viral sore throats. Your GP will decide whether they are needed. title: Viral or Bacterial Sore Throat?
h1: Is My Sore Throat Viral Or Bacterial?
description: Many people hope one symptom will tell them whether a sore throat needs antibiotics.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles is my sore throat viral or bacterial
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Cough & Sore Throat Is My Sore Throat Viral Or Bacterial? Many people hope one symptom will tell them whether a sore throat needs antibiotics. In practice, examination and sometimes testing are needed to make that judgement. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Many people hope one symptom will tell them whether a sore throat needs antibiotics. In practice, examination and sometimes testing are needed to make that judgement. What Is It? Viruses cause most sore throats and may occur with cough, runny nose or hoarseness. Streptococcal throat infection can cause fever, throat pain and tender glands, but these features are not a reliable home diagnosis. Unnecessary antibiotics can cause side effects and contribute to resistance. Fever with throat pain Swollen glands or a rash Sore throat not improving as expected Should I Be Concerned? If pain is severe, lasts longer than expected or is accompanied by fever, rash or difficulty keeping fluids down, arrange assessment. The GP may consider the full pattern of symptoms, examination and individual risk factors. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Breathing difficulty, a muffled voice with swelling, inability to swallow saliva or rapid deterioration require urgent care; call 000 if breathing is affected. Do not rely on a home visual comparison of tonsils to make an emergency decision. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can decide whether a throat swab or other tests would change management and whether antibiotic treatment is indicated. If the illness appears viral, symptom relief and monitoring may be the best approach. Before attending, note how long symptoms have lasted, whether fever or breathlessness is present and which medicines you take. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Do white spots always mean bacterial infection? No. Tonsil appearance alone does not reliably distinguish viral from bacterial illness. Will antibiotics help me recover faster? They may help in certain bacterial infections but are not useful for most viral sore throats. Benefits and risks should be assessed individually. title: When Should A Child With A Cough See A GP?
h1: When Should A Child With A Cough See A GP?
description: Children develop coughs frequently, particularly during school and childcare years.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when should a child with a cough see a gp
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Cough & Sore Throat When Should A Child With A Cough See A GP? Children develop coughs frequently, particularly during school and childcare years. Breathing, hydration and behaviour are more important than the sound of the cough alone. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Children develop coughs frequently, particularly during school and childcare years. Breathing, hydration and behaviour are more important than the sound of the cough alone. What Is It? Most childhood coughs follow viral respiratory infections. Asthma, wheeze, whooping cough and other conditions can also cause coughing. Babies and children may become unwell more quickly than adults, so age and overall appearance influence the urgency of assessment. Reduced fluids or wet nappies Cough with wheeze or fever Unusual tiredness or breathing effort Should I Be Concerned? Arrange a GP appointment if the child is worsening or not improving, has reduced drinking or fewer wet nappies, has a cough that persists beyond a few weeks, or has recurrent wheeze. A baby under three months with a fever needs prompt medical assessment. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 if the child is struggling to breathe, has blue or pale lips, is floppy or difficult to wake, or develops severe breathing pauses. Marked chest retractions, noisy breathing at rest or other signs of distress need urgent care. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess breathing effort, hydration, ears, chest and illness history, and advise on treatment and when to return. Parents can note temperature, fluid intake, breathing changes and how long the cough has lasted. Before attending, note how long symptoms have lasted, whether fever or breathlessness is present and which medicines you take. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can my child attend childcare with a cough? This depends on the illness, fever and how well the child is. Follow current childcare exclusion advice and keep an unwell child home. Are cough medicines suitable for young children? Many over-the-counter cough medicines are not recommended for young children. Ask a GP or pharmacist about age-appropriate care. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources offer further general information. title: When Should I Be Concerned About Pain?
h1: When Should I Be Concerned About Pain?
description: Pain has many causes. Learn when location, onset, changes or impact on daily activities suggest it is time to seek GP advice.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when should i be concerned about pain
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Pain & Musculoskeletal Health When Should I Be Concerned About Pain? Pain is common and has many causes. A useful assessment considers where it is, when it started, how it is changing and whether it affects normal activities. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Pain is common and has many causes. A useful assessment considers where it is, when it started, how it is changing and whether it affects normal activities. What Is It? Pain may follow an injury, inflammation, muscle strain, nerve irritation or illness. The intensity of pain alone does not identify the cause. Sudden unexplained pain, pain with fever and pain affecting movement sometimes require prompt attention. Pain changing rapidly Pain with fever or new neurological symptoms Persistent pain affecting daily life Should I Be Concerned? Arrange medical review for pain that is persistent, worsening, unexplained, recurrent or interfering with sleep, work or self-care. Tell your GP about injury, fever, numbness, weakness, medicines and any changes in bowel or bladder function. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 for chest pressure or pain suggestive of a heart attack, severe sudden abdominal pain with collapse, or pain with stroke-like symptoms. Severe pain after major trauma or with sudden loss of limb function also needs emergency assessment. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can examine the affected area, discuss likely causes and plan activity, pain relief or investigations based on clinical findings. For longer-term pain, coordinated rehabilitation and follow-up may be more useful than repeated short-term treatment. Consider noting when pain started, how it affects movement and sleep, and any treatments already tried. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Does severe pain always mean serious damage? Not always. Pain intensity and tissue injury do not always match. New severe pain still deserves assessment, especially with warning symptoms. Can I keep exercising with pain? Activity advice depends on the cause. Gentle movement is often helpful, but do not push through major injury or rapidly worsening pain. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources offer further general information. title: Muscle & Joint Pain Explained
description: Aching muscles and joints can make ordinary tasks difficult. The location, pattern and presence of swelling or stiffness help guide assessment.

text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Pain & Musculoskeletal Health Understanding Muscle And Joint Pain Aching muscles and joints can make ordinary tasks difficult. The location, pattern and presence of swelling or stiffness help guide assessment. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Aching muscles and joints can make ordinary tasks difficult. The location, pattern and presence of swelling or stiffness help guide assessment. What Is It? Muscle pain may relate to exercise, strain or illness. Joint pain may arise from osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, injury or other conditions. Morning stiffness, warmth, swelling and whether one or several joints are affected provide useful clues. Joint warmth, swelling or prolonged stiffness Muscle pain after activity or injury Pain limiting walking or daily tasks Should I Be Concerned? Book a GP review if symptoms persist, recur, limit movement, interrupt sleep or are associated with joint swelling or unexplained fatigue. Pain after a fall or injury should be assessed if walking or using the limb becomes difficult. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? A hot, swollen joint with fever needs same-day urgent assessment because infection is possible. Sudden severe pain after injury, loss of circulation or inability to bear weight may require emergency assessment. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can assess movement, swelling and medical history; advise on activity, rehabilitation and medicines; and arrange tests or referrals when indicated. Management often combines strengthening, pacing and treatment of the underlying condition. Consider noting when pain started, how it affects movement and sleep, and any treatments already tried. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Is morning stiffness important? Yes. The length and pattern of stiffness can help distinguish different joint conditions. Mention it during your appointment. Will I automatically need an X-ray? Not necessarily. Imaging is selected based on examination and the suspected cause, rather than pain alone. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources offer further general information. title: Chronic Pain: When Should I Seek Help?
h1: Chronic Pain: When Should I Seek Help?
description: Living with pain for months can affect more than the part of the body that hurts.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles chronic pain when should i seek help
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Pain & Musculoskeletal Health Chronic Pain: When Should I Seek Help? Living with pain for months can affect more than the part of the body that hurts. Sleep, mood, work and relationships may all be affected, and support remains worthwhile even when a quick cure is not available. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Living with pain for months can affect more than the part of the body that hurts. Sleep, mood, work and relationships may all be affected, and support remains worthwhile even when a quick cure is not available. What Is It? Chronic or persistent pain generally lasts beyond normal healing time, often three months or more. Pain signals may become more sensitive, and there may be several contributing factors. This does not mean the pain is imagined. Pain lasting months Pain affecting sleep, mood or work Increasing reliance on pain medicine Should I Be Concerned? Seek help when pain is persisting, medication use is increasing, function is declining or you are becoming worried about coping. Waiting until pain is severe can make the practical impact harder to manage. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? New weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control, chest pain, severe unexplained pain or pain with collapse needs emergency evaluation. If you are struggling to stay safe or have thoughts of self-harm, seek immediate help via 000 or an emergency department. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can work with you on goals such as walking, sleep, work participation and independence. Management may include physiotherapy, activity pacing, psychological strategies, medicine review and a multidisciplinary care plan where appropriate. Consider noting when pain started, how it affects movement and sleep, and any treatments already tried. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can pain continue after an injury heals? Yes. Persistent pain can involve changes in the way the nervous system processes pain. A GP can assess whether further investigation or rehabilitation is appropriate. Should I rely only on pain medicines? Usually not. Many people benefit from a combination of movement, sleep support, rehabilitation and other approaches tailored to their goals. title: Back Pain: When to See a GP
h1: Back Pain: When Should I See A GP?
description: Most episodes of back pain improve, but some need medical assessment.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles back pain when should i see a gp
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Pain & Musculoskeletal Health Back Pain: When Should I See A GP? Most episodes of back pain improve, but some need medical assessment. What matters is not just how sore the back feels but whether there are warning signs or new changes in function. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Most episodes of back pain improve, but some need medical assessment. What matters is not just how sore the back feels but whether there are warning signs or new changes in function. What Is It? Back pain may arise from muscles, joints, discs or nerves, and sometimes from conditions outside the spine. Many cases are described as non-specific back pain because a single structural cause cannot be identified. Back pain preventing ordinary activities Pain spreading to the leg Numbness, weakness or bladder changes Should I Be Concerned? See a GP if pain is not improving, significantly limits usual activities or sleep, follows an injury, or comes with pain travelling down a leg. Discuss work demands, previous episodes and what makes symptoms better or worse. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Go to emergency or call 000 for new loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around the groin, major leg weakness, fever with severe back pain or serious trauma. These symptoms can indicate conditions where delay matters. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can check movement and neurological signs and recommend a return-to-activity plan, suitable pain management, physiotherapy or investigations. Imaging is not automatically required for uncomplicated back pain. Consider noting when pain started, how it affects movement and sleep, and any treatments already tried. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Should I stay in bed? Prolonged bed rest is usually not recommended for uncomplicated back pain. Your GP can advise safe activity while symptoms settle. Does leg pain mean I need surgery? Not usually. Leg pain can occur with nerve irritation and often improves without surgery, but weakness or worsening neurological symptoms require assessment. title: Why Am I Always Tired?
description: Feeling tired from time to time is common, but ongoing fatigue that does not improve with rest can be frustrating and may deserve assessment.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles why am i always tired
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Sleep & Fatigue Why Am I Always Tired? Feeling tired from time to time is common, but ongoing fatigue that does not improve with rest can be frustrating and may deserve assessment. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Feeling tired from time to time is common, but ongoing fatigue that does not improve with rest can be frustrating and may deserve assessment. What Is It? Fatigue can reflect sleep loss, demanding schedules, stress, illness, iron deficiency, thyroid conditions, diabetes, medication effects or sleep disorders. Tiredness alone does not point to one diagnosis; associated symptoms help guide investigation. Tired despite sufficient time in bed Snoring or waking gasping Fatigue with weight, mood or menstrual changes Should I Be Concerned? Arrange GP review if fatigue lasts, worsens or affects work, parenting or daily tasks. Mention snoring, waking unrefreshed, mood changes, heavy periods, weight changes, medication use and whether sleep feels restorative. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 for fatigue with chest pain, severe breathlessness, new weakness, collapse or sudden confusion. If you are dangerously sleepy while driving, stop driving and arrange safe transport rather than trying to push through. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can review sleep and health history, examine you and choose any blood tests or referrals based on the findings. Management may involve treating an identified condition, medicine changes or sleep assessment. A brief sleep diary, information about snoring and any medicine or caffeine use can help identify patterns. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Does fatigue always mean I need blood tests? Not always. Tests depend on other symptoms, health history and examination; some causes relate to sleep or lifestyle. Can poor sleep make it hard to concentrate? Yes. Chronic sleep disruption can affect attention, memory and mood, but other medical causes should be considered if symptoms persist. title: Sleep Problems Explained
description: Sleep difficulties include more than not falling asleep.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Sleep & Fatigue Sleep Problems Explained Sleep difficulties include more than not falling asleep. Waking repeatedly, waking too early or sleeping for hours without feeling refreshed can each affect health differently. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Sleep difficulties include more than not falling asleep. Waking repeatedly, waking too early or sleeping for hours without feeling refreshed can each affect health differently. What Is It? Insomnia involves difficulty getting or staying asleep despite an opportunity to sleep. Other problems include sleep apnoea, restless legs, circadian rhythm disruption and sleep disturbed by stress, medicines, pain or menopause. Trouble falling or staying asleep Witnessed breathing pauses Sleepiness interfering with driving or work Should I Be Concerned? See a GP when sleep difficulties persist, affect daytime functioning or raise concerns about driving and work safety. Loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses or gasping during sleep suggest the need to discuss sleep apnoea. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 for severe breathing difficulty, loss of consciousness or chest pain. For daytime sleepiness that makes driving unsafe, stop driving and arrange prompt assessment; do not wait until an incident occurs. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review sleep patterns and medical causes, discuss approaches such as cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, review medicines and consider sleep-study or specialist referral when indicated. A brief sleep diary, information about snoring and any medicine or caffeine use can help identify patterns. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Are sleeping tablets the first treatment for insomnia? Not usually. Behavioural approaches, including CBT for insomnia, are important and medicines have potential risks. Does snoring always mean sleep apnoea? No, but loud snoring with pauses in breathing, choking or daytime sleepiness warrants assessment. title: When Should I Speak To A GP About Sleep?
h1: When Should I Speak To A GP About Sleep?
description: Not every restless night needs an appointment.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when should i speak to a gp about sleep
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Sleep & Fatigue When Should I Speak To A GP About Sleep? Not every restless night needs an appointment. A GP review is useful when sleep problems become a pattern or are affecting how safely and comfortably you function. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Not every restless night needs an appointment. A GP review is useful when sleep problems become a pattern or are affecting how safely and comfortably you function. What Is It? Poor sleep may involve insomnia, too little sleep, disrupted breathing, restless legs or sleep affected by physical or mental health conditions. Keeping a brief sleep diary can clarify timing, awakenings and daily impact. Sleep disruption for several weeks Daytime sleepiness or poor concentration Questions about sleep assessment and treatment Should I Be Concerned? Book a visit if symptoms persist over weeks, you regularly wake unrefreshed, fall asleep unintentionally or have loud snoring with breathing pauses. Bring details of shift work, caffeine, alcohol and any sleep medicines. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? If you are dangerously sleepy, do not drive. Call 000 if a person has severe breathing difficulty or becomes unresponsive. Urgent symptoms should not be handled through routine online booking. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can review habits and contributing conditions, identify whether a sleep study or other assessment may help, and discuss safe treatment options and follow-up. A brief sleep diary, information about snoring and any medicine or caffeine use can help identify patterns. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Should I bring a sleep diary? Yes. Notes on bedtime, waking time, daytime naps and symptoms over one or two weeks can help. Can menopause or anxiety affect sleep? Yes. Both can disturb sleep, but a GP can check for other causes rather than attributing every symptom to one factor. title: Neck Pain: When to See a GP
description: Neck pain and stiffness are common. Understand possible causes, when to see a GP and which warning signs need urgent assessment in Brisbane.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre | Pain & Musculoskeletal Health Understanding Neck Pain Neck stiffness or pain can make driving, sleeping and ordinary movement uncomfortable. Most episodes improve, but certain symptoms need medical attention. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Neck stiffness or pain can make driving, sleeping and ordinary movement uncomfortable. Most episodes improve, but certain symptoms need medical attention. This guide is general information for patients in Woolloongabba and neighbouring inner-south Brisbane communities. It does not replace an individual clinical assessment. What Is It? Neck pain refers to discomfort in the cervical spine and surrounding muscles, joints and soft tissues. It may follow an awkward sleeping position, prolonged static posture, muscle strain or an injury. Pain can also spread to the shoulders or upper back. Some neck symptoms arise from irritation of nerves in the neck. A GP assessment considers the pattern of symptoms rather than assuming that every episode needs an X-ray or scan. Should I Be Concerned? Many short episodes of mild neck pain ease with time and gentle movement. Arrange a GP review if the pain is severe, increasing, recurrent, disturbing your sleep or preventing normal activities. Neck pain after a fall or accident, or pain accompanied by fever or neurological symptoms, deserves more urgent attention. The important factors are the cause, associated symptoms and whether normal movement and strength are affected. Common Symptoms and Situations You might notice stiffness when turning your head, muscle tenderness, pain around the base of the skull, or aching that spreads into a shoulder. Some people also experience headaches. Tingling, numbness, weakness or shooting pain down an arm can suggest nerve involvement and should be discussed with a clinician. Symptoms affecting balance, walking or hand coordination need prompt assessment. If you have significant neck pain after trauma, do not try to force the neck to move or test it with stretches. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call Triple Zero (000) for severe neck pain after major trauma, or neck pain with chest pain, serious breathing difficulty, collapse or other immediately life-threatening symptoms. Keep movement limited after a significant injury until emergency help arrives. Seek urgent same-day medical assessment for neck pain with fever and marked stiffness, new arm or leg weakness, walking or balance problems, new bowel or bladder changes, or other worrying neurological symptoms. Make a routine GP appointment if neck pain continues, recurs, is getting worse or limits work, sleep and daily activities. Urgent symptoms: If someone is in immediate danger or has life-threatening symptoms, call 000. Do not use online booking for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can ask when pain started, whether there was an injury, what movements affect it, and whether there are symptoms in your arms or legs. Examination may include neck movement, strength, sensation and reflexes when indicated. Care depends on the cause and may involve advice about comfortable movement, pacing, suitable pain relief, workplace habits and physiotherapy. Imaging or specialist referral is considered when the history or examination suggests it would change management. What Happens at the Appointment? Tell the GP whether symptoms followed an accident, where the pain travels, any tingling or weakness, and what you have already tried. Note whether symptoms are worse at work, overnight or with certain movements. Your GP may discuss an activity plan and when to seek review. Ask about the safest way to return to exercise, driving, lifting and work. A scan is not automatic for uncomplicated neck pain. Frequently Asked Questions Is a stiff neck always serious? No. Mild stiffness is common. However, a stiff neck with fever, severe headache, confusion or neurological symptoms needs urgent medical assessment. Should I get a scan for neck pain? Not everyone needs imaging. Your GP will consider trauma, weakness, numbness, examination findings and whether imaging would help guide care. Can neck pain cause headaches? Yes. Some neck conditions can be associated with headaches, but headaches have many causes. New severe or unusual headaches require assessment. Can I continue moving when my neck hurts? Gentle, comfortable movement often helps uncomplicated neck pain, but the advice differs after injury or when red-flag symptoms are present. Seek individual advice if unsure.
